newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria leaders vow to track down killers of ex-pm.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria leaders vow to track down killers of ex-pm.

text.p: Bulgarian leaders vowed tough new measures to combat organised crime after the murder of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov and said plans for a presidential election later this month would not be disrupted.

The shooting of Lukanov, 58, a millionaire businessman and parliamentarian for the ruling Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), stunned the small former communist country grappling with a deep economic crisis and rising crime wave.

"The tragic case with Andrei Lukanov shows again that the fight against terrorism, organised crime and the mafia requires the united efforts of all institutions and cooperation with all countries," President Zhelyu Zhelev said.

In an address to the nation, he said Lukanov's murder should not be allowed to fuel pre-election tension and he and other politicians were adamant that the poll should go ahead as planned on October 27.

"We are witnessing another act that is destabilising the country in the decisive stage of the economic reforms on the eve of the presidential elections, which will be held on October 27," Prime Minister Zhan Videnov said in a separate broadcast address.
He pledged that the government would do everything in its power to apprehend and punish the perpetrators of the killing.
"No extraordinary measures are necessary...but further acts to strengthen social order and lawfullness," he said.
The country of 8.5 million is plagued by rising prices, a battered economy and uncertain prospects while suffering a rising crime wave.

Armed police threw up checkpoints on major roads between the Bulgarian capital and the country's borders, witnesses said. Security measures were tightened at airports, Sofia railway station and border crossing points.

The silver-haired Lukanov, a former communist politburo member in the communist era, was widely seen as a powerful man in Bulgaria although he held no official post beyond being a deputy for the ruling Socialist Party.
He was found dead of gunshot wounds in front of his Sofia home. State radio said he had been probably killed at around 9.30 a.m. (0730 GMT) on Wednesday.

Bulgarian state news agency BTA said police had arrested an elderly man who looked like a tramp near the scene of the killing. But this was not confirmed by police and it was not clear if it represented a firm lead.

National Security Service chief Dimitar Vladimirov told journalists that Lukanov had been under his unit's protection earlier this year following a specific threat. The protection ended after an "investigation clarified the case," he said.

"Lukanov's hands were holding key positions, mighty financial and political forces at home and abroad are behind him," the leader of one of the biggest trade unions Podkrepa Konstantin Trenchev told the 24 Hours newspaper's extraordinary edition.

Lukanov, one of the architects of the downfall of communist dictator Todor Zhivkov in 1989, served as communist prime minister in 1990 but resigned due to widespread public dissatisfaction with the sluggish pace of reform.
Under his rule, Bulgaria declared a moratorium on $12 billion of foreign debt.

In 1992 the public prosecutor launched an inquiry into whether Lukanov misappropriated funds in the 1980s when he was deputy prime minister. He was stripped of parliamentary rights and detained for six months until the case was dropped.
Earlier this year Lukanov criticised the Socialist Party for reviving the functions of the Stalinist state and restoring ties with the secret services.
